strengths: A well-designed closed-loop tracking pipeline that addresses a critical limitation of current 6D pose trackers, which typically operate 'blindly' and cannot recover once they lose track.

Strong performance on the standard BOP benchmark datasets, showing that the proposed SOM (Segmenting Object Module) outperforms existing zero-shot and even some fully supervised baselines in segmentation quality.
Efficient design with a runtime profile that supports real-time deployment (TOM adds only ~9.1ms of overhead, allowing steady-state tracking at 25–33 FPS on an H100).
Excellent presentation, clear visual explanations (Figures 2 and 4), and a thoroughly documented appendix containing full algorithmic details and implementation parameters.
weaknesses: High dependency on complex third-party tools such as SAM3D for geometry estimation and FoundationPose for downstream tracking, meaning the pipeline's ultimate success is highly bottlenecked by these components.

The evaluation of tracking failure recovery (stress tests) relies on synthetically corrupted datasets (manually dropping frames and overlaying random masks on YCB-Video) rather than testing on real-world natural sequence failures like complete out-of-view movements or drastic dynamic illumination changes.

Limited details on the quality of SAM3D's single-image 3D reconstructions. Since single-view 3D reconstruction is a challenging task, it remains unclear how robust the system is to geometric reconstruction errors or incomplete meshes during real-world deployments.

strengths: Unifies reference-conditioned segmentation (SOM), online tracking-loss verification (TOM), and geometric anchoring (SAM3D) into a robust, closed-loop 6D pose tracking system.
Addresses a critical limitation of modern trackers (operating 'blindly') by introducing a learned compatibility verifier (TOM) that reliably detects drift and triggers re-localization.
Demonstrates state-of-the-art results in annotation-free segmentation and 6D pose tracking on challenging datasets like LM-O, YCB-Video, and other BOP benchmarks.
Provides a thorough empirical analysis, including ablation studies on HSFA layers, language conditioning, number of reference views, and verification matching configurations.
The manuscript is highly polished, with clear architectural diagrams, well-defined formulations, and comprehensive implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The framework heavily relies on a series of large, frozen foundation models (DINOv3, SAM3D, FoundationPose, CLIP/VLMs), making it hard to decouple the success of STORM's fusion logic from the representational power of these backbones.

While the steady-state tracking loop is efficient, the re-localization stage (invoking SOM and FoundationPose re-initialization) is computationally heavy and could introduce noticeable latency spikes during persistent tracking failures in real-time robotic tasks.

The synthetic dataset used to train TOM relies on simple 2D crop shifting and random cropping, which may not fully capture the complex, non-linear visual deformations and perspective shifts seen during actual 3D tracking drift.
The performance gains from injecting VLM-derived semantic priors are marginal in most quantitative evaluations (e.g., Table 7), indicating that visual matching dominates the alignment process.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem in 6D object tracking: detecting tracking drift and establishing a closed-loop recovery mechanism without relying on manual resets.
The framework integrates multiple modalities (2D appearance, text prompts, and 3D geometry) into a unified pipeline.
The proposed Segmenting Object Module (SOM) shows strong quantitative performance (high Average Precision) on several BOP datasets compared to existing zero-shot baselines.
weaknesses: The paper contains several critical presentation issues and broken placeholders. Figure 5 and Figure 7 are completely blank with missing plot images. Additionally, Footnote 1 on page 2 contains an empty code link ('Code available at .'). This indicates an incomplete draft.

The core components of the pipeline heavily rely on frozen, pre-trained external models (such as FoundationPose for 6D tracking, SAM3D for mesh reconstruction, DINOv3, and CLIP/LLM). The actual technical contribution of the proposed modules (HSFA and TOM) is relatively marginal, consisting of standard cross-attention blocks and a lightweight binary classification head.

The framing of the tracking verification as an 'energy-like score' is misleading. The model is trained with standard binary cross-entropy (BCE) and uses the negative sigmoid logit at inference time. There is no actual energy-based model training or optimization, making the energy terminology feel like unnecessary jargon.

There is a contradiction in the CAD-free claim. Although the method claims to operate without curated CAD models, Table 3 shows that without aligning the SAM3D-reconstructed model to the ground-truth CAD model using ICP, the pose estimation accuracy (ADD-SAUC) drops drastically from 99.12 to 44.92. This indicates that the reported benchmark performance still relies heavily on the presence of the CAD models for coordinate alignment.

The SOM module is trained on the training splits of the evaluated BOP datasets (LM-O, T-LESS, TUD-L, HB, YCB-V). Since the same object identities are shared between the train and test splits, the claimed 'zero-shot' generalization capability of the reference-conditioned segmentation is weakened.

strengths: The paper addresses two crucial and practical limitations in current 6D object pose tracking: the reliance on manual initialization masks and the inability to recover from tracking failures (e.g., due to rapid motion or heavy occlusions).

STORM is a highly unified and complete pipeline integrating rendering, LLM-based semantic prompt generation, a novel Hierarchical Spatial Fusion Attention (HSFA) mechanism, foundation segmentation models, and an active tracking failure recovery module (TOM).

Strong empirical performance: The proposed Segmenting Object Module (SOM) achieves state-of-the-art results on several challenging BOP datasets, outperforming other zero-shot and even some supervised methods.

Comprehensive ablation studies are provided, demonstrating the effectiveness and trade-offs of individual components, such as the language injection module, the number of attention layers in HSFA, and the tracking-loss classifier configuration.
weaknesses: The figures showing training curves and ablation results (Figures 5, 6, and 7) have very small, blurry, and overlapping text, making the legends and axes difficult to read.

The tracking failure evaluation relies primarily on synthetically generated scenarios (e.g., frame-dropping and random masking on YCB-Video). Testing on real physical tracking sequences with challenging motion and complex real-world occlusions would provide stronger validation.

There is a lack of detailed analysis on the latency overhead when tracking failure is detected and re-registration is triggered. Given that the SOM module takes 183ms to infer, a sudden drop to ~5 FPS during re-registration could impact real-time robotic control, which should be discussed.
Some typos and confusing references exist in the text, such as the LLM named 'gemma-3n-E4B-it' (which seems like an unconventional or corrupted name) and reference formatting issues in the tables.

strengths: STORM presents a complete, annotation-free pipeline for joint 6D pose estimation and tracking, which removes the need for manual initialization masks.

The addition of a dedicated Tracking Object Module (TOM) successfully addresses a major limitation of current trackers (like FoundationPose) by detecting tracking drift/failures and triggering re-registration.
Strong quantitative results on standard benchmarks (such as LMO and YCB-Video) for zero-shot object segmentation and pose tracking.
weaknesses: There are several notable presentation and polish issues throughout the paper. For instance, Figure 5 is extremely small and illegible. Figures 6 and 7 contain corrupted characters in their legends (e.g., '一 HSFA7e'). Algorithm 1 contains spelling mistakes (e.g., 'region of intrest' on line 21).

The model name 'gemma-3n-E4B-it' (on page 3) is highly anomalous and appears to be a typo or an AI-generated placeholder, which raises questions about the rigor and reproducibility of the language guidance component.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental. The framework relies heavily on existing heavyweight modules (DINOv2, SAM2, FoundationPose), and the proposed additions (HSFA and AdaNorm-Zero) are standard spatial attention and normalization modifications.

The paper lacks a thorough analysis of the computational latency during an active recovery phase. While the tracking failure detection (TOM) is fast, executing the full re-registration (SOM + FoundationPose initialization) upon tracking loss will likely introduce significant latency spikes, disrupting real-time deployment.

The motivation for incorporating LLM-generated semantic descriptions is weak. The ablation study shows a marginal accuracy improvement (Table 5) at a high computational cost (increasing inference time from 0.196s to 0.265s), but does not compare against simple text templates (e.g., 'a photo of [class]').

strengths: STORM presents a complete, practical, and annotation-free pipeline for 6D object pose estimation and tracking, which is highly valuable for real-world robotics applications.

The proposed Tracking Object Module (TOM) successfully addresses a major limitation of current 6D trackers (like FoundationPose) by introducing an automated tracking failure detection and re-registration mechanism.
The proposed method achieves impressive state-of-the-art results on several challenging BOP datasets (LM-O, YCB-V, T-LESS, etc.) for zero-shot/unsupervised segmentation.
The paper includes extensive ablation studies and provides a detailed appendix detailing the HSFA algorithm and implementation parameters.
weaknesses: The quality of the figures (specifically Figures 5, 6, and 7) is very poor. The plots are extremely small, with blurry and unreadable axis labels and legends, which hinders the readability of the ablation studies.
There is a typo in a section title on page 3: 'Object Segementation from a Single 3D Model'.

The paper claims to run in 'real-time', but Table 2 shows that the Segmenting Object Module (SOM) takes 0.183 seconds (around 5.5 FPS) per frame. While the TOM tracking is fast, if a failure occurs, the recovery/re-registration process will introduce a noticeable lag (at ~5 FPS), which might be problematic for high-speed robotic tasks.
The reference to 'gemma-3n-E4B-it' (Team 2025) is unclear. It is not a widely recognized public model name and should be clarified.

The combination of Tversky loss and Focal loss is described as a 'novel loss formulation', but similar hybrid losses (e.g., Focal Tversky loss) have been extensively used in medical image segmentation and are well-established in the literature.
